This excerpt describes a speech given by Frederick Douglass in 1841.

I attended an anti-slavery convention . . . at which it was my happiness to become acquainted with Frederick Douglass. . . .

I shall never forget his first speech at the convention—the powerful impression it created. . . . I think I never hated slavery so intensely as at that moment. . . .

. . . He came forward to the platform with a hesitancy and embarrassment. . . . After apologizing for his ignorance, and reminding the audience that slavery was a poor school for the human intellect and heart, he proceeded to narrate some of the facts in his own history as a slave.

—William Lloyd Garrison, from Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave by Frederick Douglass

options.label: A
options.text: He was elected as a state government official who challenged the system of slavery.

options.label: B
options.text: He formed relationships with those who had different views on slavery from his own.

options.label: C
options.text: He described his own personal experiences under the system of slavery.

options.label: D
options.text: He emphasized that an educational system was the main way to end slavery.

notes: This is Part A of a multipart question. The response contains only Part A as requested.
